newsitem.title: UK: Storm of speculation over GEC shake-up plan.
newsitem.headline: Storm of speculation over GEC shake-up plan.

text.p: Britain's General Electric Co Plc was caught up in a storm of speculation on Monday ahead of its long-awaited strategic review, with rumours ranging from major sell-offs to full-blown takeover bids.
Tuesday will be make-or-break time for the British engineering giant as George Simpson, managing director, publishes his plan to take GEC into the next century.

The review comes against a backdrop of mounting pressure for the European defence industry to consolidate after mega-mergers in the U.S. between Lockheed Martin Corp and Northrop Grumman Corp plus Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas .
Analysts and press reports put forward a range of possibilities for GEC to move forward.
Top of the list was the reappearance of rumours of a possible merger between GEC and its old adversary British Aerospace Plc.

GEC refused to comment. But Bae spokesman Simon Raynes, spokesman at BAe told Reuters, "We are in favour of consolidation of aerospace and defence in Europe. But we are ruling nothing in and nothing out."

BAe admitted the U.S. deals had concentrated European minds even more. "The pace of consolidation in the U.S. reminds us that we in Europe must move as fast as we can," said Raynes. Bae shares rose 14 pence to 13.26-1/2 pounds, while GEC was down 3-1/2 at 376-1/2 pence.
Another GEC takeover rumour on Monday was a story in The Times predicting GEC will buy Italy's defence group Alenia Difensa. Alenia is controlled by the state-owned Finmeccanica SpA.

GEC and Finmeccanica announced in May that their joint study on linking up in the defence industry was making good progress. The two companies had said in a statement they were in contact "at the highest level".
Analysts said takeover bid stories had gained currency following shock departure of finance director David Newlands who quit last week.

The move added spice to speculation of a bold shake-up and was interpreted as a signal that Simpson is moving in his own men and finally stepping out of the shadow of his predecessor, veteran boss Lord Weinstock.

"We don't know what Simpson will announce. But one thing is clear -- it will be something dramatic, specially now that there has been a boardroom struggle and Simpson has won," said analyst Andy Crispin at SocGen.
Another added "This clears the way for a possible deal with British Aerospace."
Away from the bid rumours, many analysts believe that GEC will focus its attention on its defence-electronics arm GEC-Marconi and possibly sell off its two other joint-venture businesses.

They are GEC-Alsthom, the Anglo-French rail and power joint venture and GPT which is a jointly owned telecoms group with Siemens Plc, the British arm of Siemens AG. GEC owns 60 percent of GPT, with 40 percent held by Siemens.

But GEC is also on the final bid shortlist for Siemens' defence business which is currently up for sale. This scenario has fuelled rumours that GEC will negotiate an asset swap of its 60 percent stake in GPT in return for the Siemens defence business.
A spokesman for Siemens told Reuters that it was very pleased with the performance of the telecoms business and wanted to expand in that sector.
"We are happy with the way things are going. Telecoms is one of our core business areas and any opportunity to strengthen it we would consider seriously," said the Siemens Plc spokesman .
He added that in April Siemens took management control of GPT's private communications division which provides internal company telecoms systems.
"We now have 50 percent plus one controlling share in the company named Siemens GEC Communications," he said.
Through the haze of rumours, one thing remains clear -- with around 1.3 billion pounds ($2.2 billion) in free cash GEC has huge financial scope for deal-making.

But one industry insider and former GEC employee told Reuters even if Simpson was radical on Tuesday, he would have a tough job on his hands to get things moving after so many years of GEC drifting in strategic slumber.
"It's like trying to wake up an elephant, get it to shift in a different direction and then persuade it to move in that direction. Not an easy job," he said.
